attempts.raw_response: The construction of the dam transformed the natural wetland into a complex network of canals and lakes, creating an ideal habitat for diverse aquatic life. This artificial ecosystem quickly became renowned for its abundant fish populations, particularly the famous carp, which attracted anglers from across the region. Over the decades, the area evolved into a significant economic hub for local communities who relied heavily on fishing and related industries. Today, Bueng Boraphet remains a vital ecological zone, supporting not only commercial fisheries but also migratory birds and other wildlife. The interplay between human activity and nature has shaped its current landscape, making it a unique example of how infrastructure can inadvertently create new biodiversity hotspots while sustaining traditional livelihoods in central Thailand.

pair.human_continuation:
This is the only known site for the white-eyed river martin which used to winter there, but has not been seen since 1980, and may be extinct.

Once in the past Siamese tiger perch can be considered the most famous fish species here, until it was said that "If anyone comes to Bueng Borapet and doesn't eat this species of fish it is as if that person has never arrived". But now it is probably  completely extinct in Bueng Boraphet, from being caught too much, both for consumption and for trade in the aquarium fish industry.

A near-threatened species, the marsh grassbird, was first discovered in Thailand here in early December 2019.

One hundred and six square kilometres of the lake were declared a non-hunting area in 1975.
pair.prefix:
Bueng Boraphet (, , lit. "giloy swamp") is the largest freshwater swamp and lake in central Thailand. It covers an area of 224 km2 east of Nakhon Sawan, south of the Nan River close to its confluence with the Ping River. This swamp can be seen from the train window between Bueng Boraphet and Thap Krit stations on the Northern railway line.

Originally the area was covered by a large swamp, which was flooded in 1930 with the building of a dam to improve fishing.
